sectors.title: Technology
sectors.summary: Software, product, design and data. There's far more of this work in Ireland than you'd expect, and a lot of it is in Irish companies most people haven't heard of. A computer science degree is the usual way in, but it isn't the only one. There are apprenticeships too, though they're rarely advertised, and after your first job hardly anyone asks where you studied.

sectors.title: Healthcare
sectors.summary: Medicine, nursing, physiotherapy, pharmacy, occupational therapy, and plenty of jobs that never come up in careers talks. It's some of the most stable work in the country. The ways in vary more than students expect. Some people go straight from the Leaving Cert, others take a conversion course ten years later.

sectors.title: Law
sectors.summary: Solicitor, barrister, legal executive, or working in-house for a company. The usual path is a law degree and then professional exams. Graduate entry from other degrees is common too, and the legal executive route doesn't need a degree at all. Firms range from big Dublin practices to one-solicitor offices, and the work is very different in each.

sectors.title: Finance
sectors.summary: Banking, accountancy, insurance, fintech and the public sector. Several accounting qualifications can be done while you're working and getting paid, so you earn while you train.

sectors.title: Trades
sectors.summary: Some of the most in-demand work in the country, and some of the least explained. You get in through a SOLAS apprenticeship, paid from year one with no college fees, and you're qualified in about four years. It offers long-term security, the option to work for yourself, and a path into contracting and running sites.

sectors.title: Media & communications
sectors.summary: Journalism, broadcasting, PR, marketing and content. Journalism and broadcasting are long-established, while the rest moves fast. There are courses for all of it. You can also get in by building up a body of work until someone notices, which is harder than it sounds but more common than it used to be.

sectors.title: Education
sectors.summary: Teaching, special education, youth work, further education and educational psychology. Primary teaching has its own degree. Secondary teaching is usually a subject degree and then a masters. Youth and community work has routes in that don't need a traditional degree, but they're rarely mentioned.

sectors.title: Engineering
sectors.summary: Civil, mechanical, electrical, biomedical and manufacturing. Ireland does a lot of medical device and pharmaceutical manufacturing. You can get in through a degree or a higher apprenticeship, and technician routes offer a paid way in without four years of college first.

sectors.title: Public sector
sectors.summary: The civil service, local councils, An Garda Síochána, the Defence Forces and state agencies. A lot of jobs are filled through open competitions rather than degree requirements. The Leaving Cert is enough for several entry grades, with a clear way up after that.

sectors.title: Other sectors
sectors.summary: Mentors whose work doesn't fit neatly into the sectors above, such as agriculture, hospitality, the arts, sport, logistics and charities.
